title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What is the lesson of IBM's 2023-to-2026 reversal? `[V]`
options: That AI automation of HR work does not deliver its promised savings
That capacity you do not deliberately redeploy gets stranded — and the pipeline is the first thing you lose and the last thing you can rebuild
That entry-level roles are more resistant to automation than expected
That headcount reductions should be announced only after results are proven
questions.explanation: The obvious reading is wrong: AskHR worked, and this track relies on it twice. The story is about what happened to the capacity. Everything else can be re-hired at market rate; a three-year gap in junior intake cannot.

questions.prompt: How should the Gartner rehiring figure be characterized? `[V]`
options: A finding that half of AI-driven headcount reductions have already been reversed

A prediction — that by 2027 half the companies attributing cuts to AI will rehire under different titles — concerning customer service rather than HR, and against a base where only ~20% made such cuts
An observation specific to HR shared services
A regulatory forecast with compliance implications
questions.explanation: Forecast, not observation; customer service, not HR; and the base rate cuts against the discourse — most organizations held staffing flat while absorbing more volume.

questions.prompt: Why does the reinvestment commitment belong inside the enablement decision?
options: Because auditors require it to be documented at approval
Because it behaves like the kill condition — nearly free to write before anyone is invested, nearly impossible afterwards
Because finance will not approve the business case without it
Because it determines the 90-day measure
questions.explanation: Module 2's argument arriving one level up. "We will redeploy to higher-value work" means nobody has decided, and it will still mean that in eighteen months.

questions.prompt: Where does an AI agent belong in an org structure, per the emerging convention? `[V]`
options: As a headcount entry with a cost centre, so its expense is visible
In a separate agent hierarchy parallel to the human one
Nowhere on the human reporting chart — what goes on the chart is the accountable human owner who answers for its outputs
Wherever the vendor's implementation guide recommends
questions.explanation: Which is Module 1's accountability column and Module 7's signature arriving from org design. The chart question resolves into the register question. Roughly 31% of leaders are already framing AI as a teammate, so this is being decided with or without you.

questions.prompt: What quietly breaks in reporting when work moves to agents?
options: Headcount reconciliation between the HCM and payroll
Span of control, cost per employee and revenue per employee — because the work moved and the denominators didn't, so the ratios now measure something different from last year
Effective-dated history for affected positions
Manager hierarchy integrity
questions.explanation: And nobody will announce it. You are the person who will be asked why the numbers moved, which is a good reason to have decided the treatment deliberately and written it down.

questions.prompt: What is the fourth term of the bet, available only to this role?
options: The reinvestment commitment
The review date and its owner
What you would turn off
The named accountable human
questions.explanation: No other role in the curriculum can subtract — an HRBP cannot retire a process, a recruiter cannot disable an integration. And subtraction reduces the surface every other module has to govern, which usually makes the widest-reach unowned capability in your register the best available bet.

questions.prompt: What single test distinguishes a bet from a migration?
options: Whether a baseline was recorded before launch
Whether there is a state of the world in which you do not proceed
Whether the change is reversible within a quarter
Whether the vendor contract includes a termination right
questions.explanation: If the vendor is signed, the date announced and the training built, it is a migration — which is legitimate and should be called one. Using "bet" for something that cannot go either way is how a function loses the ability to stop anything.

questions.prompt: What does the module conclude from HR's absence from AI strategy in 52% of organizations? `[V]`
options: That the function should campaign for a seat at the strategy table
That AI governance should be owned by IT instead

That the function is excluded from strategy while its systems are where the AI actually runs — so this role holds an implementation-layer seat the function's leadership often lacks, with artifacts nobody else can produce
That HR technology adoption figures are overstated
questions.explanation: Read against Module 1's finding that HR technology is the second-most-adopted area in the function. Not the back office: the control surface — the only place the function's AI can actually be governed.
